questions.q: Why can't you implement a classical-style 'checkpoint and restore' for an arbitrary unknown quantum state?
options: Checkpointing works fine for quantum states; the lesson is wrong to suggest otherwise
A checkpoint is effectively a clone, and no-cloning proves no operation can duplicate an arbitrary unknown quantum state
Quantum states are too large in memory to ever be saved
Checkpointing only fails for entangled states, not single qubits
questions.explain: A checkpoint-and-restore pattern requires making a duplicate copy to fall back on, which is exactly what the no-cloning theorem (Lesson 21) proves is impossible for an arbitrary unknown state.

questions.q: How does quantum error correction work around the no-cloning constraint, rather than violating it?
options: It makes several identical classical copies of the qubit's state and compares them
Quantum error correction is impossible, so quantum computers cannot correct errors at all
It avoids the problem by measuring the logical qubit directly after every operation

It spreads one logical qubit's information across many entangled physical qubits and detects/corrects errors via joint 'syndrome' measurements, without ever cloning or directly revealing the logical state
questions.explain: Error correction uses redundancy across entangled physical qubits combined with syndrome measurements that reveal error information without revealing or copying the protected logical state -- a genuinely different strategy than classical redundancy, required because cloning isn't an option.

questions.q: Why does no-cloning make eavesdropping on a quantum key distribution channel detectable?
options: Because quantum key distribution does not actually rely on no-cloning in any way

An eavesdropper cannot clone an intercepted qubit to keep a copy while passing an undisturbed original onward, and cannot measure it without risking disturbing it -- so interception leaves a statistically detectable trace
Because quantum channels are physically impossible to intercept at all
Because eavesdroppers are always classical and therefore cannot interact with qubits
questions.explain: An eavesdropper's best strategy -- clone first, then measure the clone while passing the original on untouched -- is exactly what no-cloning forbids. Attempting to extract information instead by directly measuring risks disturbing the state, which the legitimate parties can detect.

questions.q: What is the core asymmetry between classical and quantum information that no-cloning creates?
options: Classical bits cannot be copied at all, while quantum bits can be copied freely
There is no real asymmetry; both can be copied under the right conditions
Quantum bits can be copied, but only if they are first converted to classical bits
Classical bits can be copied perfectly and silently as a basic operation, while quantum states provably cannot -- a structural difference, not an engineering gap in either direction
questions.explain: Classical computing and networking are built on the assumption that copying bits is free and perfect; quantum information structurally cannot be copied this way, which is a fundamentally different kind of information, not an inferior version of classical bits.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say quantum error correction must be 'designed from day one' around no-cloning, rather than treated as an exception to patch in later?
options: Because no-cloning is expected to be disproven once quantum hardware improves
Because quantum error correction and no-cloning are unrelated topics

Because the classical redundancy strategy (keep identical copies) is unavailable from the start for quantum states, so any viable error-correction scheme has to use a fundamentally different mechanism from the ground up
Because error correction is only needed for classical bits stored inside a quantum computer
questions.explain: Since cloning a state to keep a backup copy is never an option, any error-correction approach has to be built around redundancy strategies (like spreading information across entangled qubits) that don't require ever violating no-cloning -- it's a design constraint from the start, not an afterthought.
